issues.description: keyPressEvent complects the toggle check, key dispatch, and hide-and-forward action in one branch
issues.detail: The new guard intertwines three concerns: reading config, classifying the key (Tab vs not-Tab), and the side effect of hiding plus forwarding to the textedit. A small pure predicate like `should_accept(key, use_enter)` returning a value, with the side-effecting branch downstream, would separate decision from action and read at the call site instead of mid-loop.

issues.description: The accept-key set is implicit and scattered rather than represented as data
issues.detail: What keys accept a completion is a fact about the world; right now it is encoded as `not key == Qt.Key_Tab` plus whatever the enclosing branch already matched on. A small data value -- e.g. `accept_keys = {Tab} if not use_enter else {Tab, Enter, Return}` -- makes the policy a value you can read, test, and change, instead of a conditional buried in an event handler.

`not key == Qt.Key_Tab` parses awkwardly and only excludes one key; if Enter, Return, and Tab are the real value set, say so. `key != Qt.Key_Tab` is the familiar form, but the deeper fix is to name the set of accept keys explicitly rather than expressing the rule by negation of one constant.

issues.description: Config key `use_enter_for_completions` conflates the policy with one keystroke
issues.detail: The flag names a mechanism (Enter), not the concept (which keys accept a completion). If Return, Enter on numpad, or other accept keys ever matter, this name will lie. A name like `completion_accept_keys` (data) or at minimum `accept_completion_with_enter` keeps the value-level meaning visible and avoids baking a single key into the schema.

issues.description: `get_conf` called inside the hot keyPressEvent path each keystroke
issues.detail: Reading configuration on every key press complects a slow-changing identity (user preference) with a fast-changing one (keystrokes). The preference is a value that changes rarely; subscribing once and caching as an attribute would separate the time semantics and make the event handler about keys, not about config lookup.

review.summary: The change is small and the behavior reasonable, but it adds an incidental conditional into an already busy keyPressEvent rather than separating the question ("which keys accept?") from the action ("hide and forward"). The accept policy is a value -- a small set of keys -- and would be simpler as data than as a negated equality check buried in an event handler. The config name bakes one keystroke (Enter) into the schema where the underlying concept is the accept-key set. None of this blocks the fix; the question that should have been asked first is "what is the set of keys that accept a completion, and where does that value live?"
